title: Computer-Use & Voice Agents

techniques.name: Screen-Understanding GUI Agents
techniques.q: Can an agent use an app the way a person does?
techniques.what: A computer-use agent looks at screenshots, decides where to click or what to type, acts through mouse and keyboard actions, and takes another screenshot to check. It can drive legacy desktop or terminal applications that have no API. Each step can fail, and failures compound over long tasks, so reliable GUI agents verify after actions, zoom into small text, use accessibility information where available, and are replaced by an API wherever one exists.

techniques.name: Browser Automation Agents
techniques.q: Should the agent read the page or look at it?
techniques.what: Browser agents act on websites through a controlled browser. They can observe a page as screenshots, raw HTML or an accessibility tree; the tree gives roles, names and stable references in a few thousand tokens and is usually the best default, with screenshots added for visual layout. Hybrid designs script the known steps such as navigation and login in code and let the agent handle what varies, which is cheaper and more reliable than a fully autonomous agent.

pitfalls: Feeding raw HTML to the model

tools: Browserbase or Steel for hosted browsers
techniques.remember: Read the tree, script what is fixed, let the agent handle the rest.

techniques.name: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
techniques.q: How fast must a voice agent answer, and in which language?
techniques.what: A voice agent either chains speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, or uses a speech-to-speech model. Callers expect a reply within about 600 ms of finishing; beyond 1.5 s the call feels broken. Every stage streams, turn detection decides when the caller has finished, and callers must be able to interrupt. In India the harder problem is language: accuracy in Hindi is far better than in Bhojpuri or Maithili, code-mixed Hinglish is the norm, and phone audio degrades recognition further.

Outbound reminders and collections calls
Voice interfaces in apps
steps: Measure latency from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio
Use smart turn detection and streaming at every stage
Choose speech models evaluated on your callers’ languages and phone audio
Allow barge-in and hand over to a person when confidence is low
pitfalls: Silence-based turn detection that waits 800 ms
Choosing speech-to-text on clean benchmarks rather than real calls
No human fallback for low-resource languages
tools: OpenAI Realtime API and Gemini Live API
techniques.remember: Stream everything, detect turns smartly, test on real callers.

techniques.name: Multimodal Inputs
techniques.q: How should the agent read documents, images and screenshots?
techniques.what: Multimodal models read images directly: scanned documents, phone photos, screenshots and charts. Quality depends on the input: deskewing, cropping and resizing to the model’s limits matter, and small text may need tiling or zoom. For fields that matter, such as KYC details or claim amounts, a second reader such as OCR or a second model cross-checks the first, and disagreements go to a person.

pitfalls: Sending huge images that the API downscales anyway

tools: Claude, GPT and Gemini vision models

techniques.remember: Clean the image, read it twice, check the fields.

techniques.name: Safety for Agents that Act on Screens
techniques.q: What stops a screen agent from doing damage?
techniques.what: An agent that clicks and types can pay, submit, delete and send. Web pages and screens can carry injected instructions, and mistakes on irreversible actions cannot be undone. Safe designs run the agent in an isolated VM or browser without personal profiles, restrict it to an allowlist of sites, keep credentials in a vault so the model never sees them, screen observations for injection, require human confirmation for irreversible actions, cap steps and spend, and record every session.

Agents with access to payment or admin screens

metrics: dedicated VM or container, minimal privileges

steps: Isolate the environment and remove personal data
Allowlist domains and actions
Inject credentials outside the model
Confirm irreversible actions and record everything
pitfalls: Running the agent in someone’s everyday browser
Letting on-screen text act as instructions
Confirmation prompts so frequent that people approve blindly
tools: VMs or containers for the agent
techniques.remember: Isolate, allowlist, never show secrets, confirm what cannot be undone.

techniques.name: Evaluating Computer-Use Agents
techniques.q: How do we know it works, beyond a scoreboard?
techniques.what: OSWorld tests agents on 369 real desktop and web tasks in virtual machines, with success checked by scripts; WebArena tests 812 tasks on self-hosted websites such as shops, forums and GitLab. They show general capability, but scores are mostly self-reported and depend on the scaffolding. For production, build an evaluation on your own tasks in a staging replica, check outcomes rather than clicks, run each task several times to measure reliability, and include injected pages and irreversible actions.

techniques.name: Speech in Indian Languages
techniques.q: Does the agent hear Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish correctly?
techniques.what: Speech recognition and synthesis for Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other Indian languages, including callers who switch between them and English mid-sentence. Accuracy differs widely by language, accent and channel: an English-first model that is fine on English can get half the words wrong in Tamil on an 8 kHz phone line. The work is choosing an Indic-tuned recogniser, identifying the language turn by turn, boosting your own vocabulary, turning spoken amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar” into ₹3,500, and measuring word error rate per language on your own call recordings. Latency and the voice loop itself belong to Realtime Voice Agents; this is about language quality.

steps: Sample and transcribe your own calls, stratified by language, accent and channel
Identify the language on every turn and route to a recogniser tuned for it and for 8 kHz audio
Add custom vocabulary and rules that turn spoken amounts into numbers, then read them back
Report WER per language and amount accuracy, and hand low-confidence turns to a person

techniques.remember: Measure per language on your own calls. Identify each turn, boost your words, read amounts back.

techniques.name: Telephony and Contact-Centre Integration
techniques.q: How does a voice agent plug into real phone lines and a contact centre?
techniques.what: A voice agent in a lab talks to a browser microphone; in production it must answer phone calls. Calls arrive over the public phone network or a SIP trunk from a provider such as Exotel, Plivo or Twilio, and the provider streams 8 kHz audio to the agent over a WebSocket or bridges it into a media server such as LiveKit. The agent needs call control (answer, hold, DTMF keypad input, hang up), a warm transfer that passes a summary to a human agent in the contact centre, call recording with consent, and logging into the CRM. In India, media routed through distant regions adds delay, and outbound calling must follow TRAI’s commercial-communication rules, including do-not-disturb preferences and designated number series. This is an educational summary; confirm current telecom rules. Latency budgets and speech models are covered by the Voice Agents and Speech in Indian Languages techniques.

pitfalls: Media bouncing through a US region, adding a quarter-second to every turn

techniques.remember: Stream the call close to the caller; transfer warm; respect the rules.

TOOLS = [{"type": "computer_toolset_20260801"}]                     #@1

def run_task(task, vm, max_steps=40):                                  #@5
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):                                         #@5
        response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5",
            max_tokens=2048, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)           #@2
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use": continue
            output = vm.execute(block.name, block.input)    # click, type  #@3
            shot = vm.screenshot(max_long_edge=1568)        # look again   #@4
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": [output, shot]})                  #@4
        if not results:
            return messages                                               #@6
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise TimeoutError("step budget exhausted; hand to a person")       #@6
steps: Give the model a computer
The computer-use toolset exposes screenshot, zoom, click, type, key, scroll and wait actions. Your code executes them in a VM.
The model looks and decides
It reads the latest screenshot and returns the next action, with coordinates in the screenshot’s pixel space.
Your code acts
The harness performs the click or keystroke in the VM, scaling coordinates back to the real screen.
Look again after every action
A fresh screenshot shows whether the click worked. Without it, a wrong state goes unnoticed and errors compound.
Cap the steps
An 18-step task with checks needs about 24 actions; a budget of 20 would run out. Budget for verification.
Finish or hand over
When the model stops asking for actions, the task is done; if the budget runs out, a person takes over.

steps: A browser you control
Playwright runs a clean browser with no personal profile. The agent never uses anyone’s everyday browser.
Script the fixed route
Navigation, search and login never change from day to day, so they are plain code: fast, cheap and reliable.
Read the accessibility tree
A snapshot lists roles, names and links in about 3,000 tokens, against about 25,000 for raw HTML.
The agent decides what varies
Only the judgement goes to the model: which notice is today’s corporate action. It answers with a role and a name.
Stay on the allowlist
Before following a link, the code checks the domain. A link to an unknown site is refused.
Extract into a schema
The notice becomes a typed record, such as record date and ratio, validated before it reaches the system.

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(instructions=(                                  #@5

async def entrypoint(ctx):
    session = AgentSession(
        stt=sarvam.STT(language="hi-IN"),        # tested on phone audio  #@3
        llm=openai.LLM(model="gpt-4.1-mini"),    # fast first token       #@2
        tts=sarvam.TTS(target_language_code="hi-IN"),                    #@2
        vad=silero.VAD.load(),                                           #@4
        turn_detection=MultilingualModel())      # not just silence       #@4
    await session.start(room=ctx.room, agent=Helpline())                 #@1
    await session.generate_reply(instructions="Greet the caller in Hindi.")  #@1
steps: Measure the right gap
Latency is timed from the end of the caller’s speech to the first audio back. The pilot took about 1.9 seconds, and 1 in 6 callers hung up.
Stream every stage
Speech-to-text runs while the caller talks, the model streams tokens, and synthesis starts on the first words. A fast model keeps the first token quick.
Choose speech models on real calls
A general model got 1 word in 5 wrong on Hinglish phone calls; an India-tuned model tested on recorded calls did far better.
Detect turns smartly
Waiting for 800 ms of silence adds most of a second. A turn-detection model decides sooner and lets callers interrupt.
Short, natural replies
One or two short sentences in the caller’s own mix of Hindi and English sound natural and finish sooner.
Know when to hand over
Recognition is much weaker in Bhojpuri and Maithili. When confidence is low, the agent asks once, then transfers to a person.

def preprocess(path):
    img = cv2.imread(path)
    img = deskew(crop_to_document(img))                                 #@1
    scale = 1568 / max(img.shape[:2])                                    #@2
    img = cv2.resize(img, None, fx=scale, fy=scale)                      #@2
    return cv2.imencode(".jpg", img)[1].tobytes()

def read(path):
    jpg = preprocess(path)
    fields = vision_extract(jpg, schema=ClaimDocument)                   #@3
    ocr_text = pytesseract.image_to_string(to_array(jpg), lang="hin+eng+mar")  #@4
    disagreements = [f for f in ("total_amount", "bill_date", "patient_name")
                     if not appears_in(fields[f], ocr_text)]             #@4
    if disagreements:                                                   #@5
        return {"status": "review", "fields": fields, "check": disagreements}  #@5
    return {"status": "accepted", "fields": fields}                      #@6
steps: Straighten and crop
Phone photos are tilted and include the table they sit on. Deskewing and cropping to the document gives the model a clean page.
Resize to the model’s limit
Very large images are downscaled by the API anyway; resizing yourself keeps text as legible as possible within the limit.
Read into a schema
The vision model extracts named, typed fields, so its output can be validated rather than parsed from prose.
Read it again, differently
OCR independently reads the same image. Amounts, dates and names must appear in both readings.
Disagreements go to a person
When the two readers disagree, an assessor checks the document. Most errors are caught here.
Accept the rest
Documents where both agree go straight through. Wrong amounts reaching the claims system fell below 3%.

ALLOWED = {"ops.bank.internal", "portal.vendor.example"}               #@2
IRREVERSIBLE = ("pay", "confirm", "submit", "reverse", "delete")

def check(self, action):
    self.steps += 1
    if self.steps > self.max_steps:                                     #@6
        return {"deny": "step limit reached"}                            #@6
    if urlparse(self.s.current_url).hostname not in ALLOWED:            #@2
        return {"deny": "domain not on the allowlist"}                   #@2
    if action["name"] == "left_click":
        label = self.s.element_label_at(action["input"]["coordinate"]).lower()
        if any(w in label for w in IRREVERSIBLE):                        #@5
            if not self.approver.confirm(label, self.s.screenshot()):     #@5
                return {"deny": "person declined"}
    if action["name"] == "type" and self.s.focused_is_password():         #@3
        self.s.fill_from_vault()             # the model never sees it    #@3
        return {"handled": "credential filled"}
    self.s.record(action)                                                #@6
    return {"allow": True}

steps: Isolate the agent
It runs in its own VM or browser with no staff profile, cookies or files. A mistake cannot reach anyone’s real accounts.
Allow only what the task needs
Three domains, checked before every action. The injected banner linked elsewhere, and the link was refused.
Keep secrets out of the model
When the agent reaches a password field, the harness fills it from a vault. The password never appears in a prompt or log.
Screen text is data
On-screen text such as “click Confirm Reversal” is content to read, not an instruction. Classifiers flag likely injections.
Confirm the irreversible
Clicks on pay, confirm, submit, reverse or delete need a person’s approval. Only those, so approvers stay attentive.
Limit and record
A step cap stops runaway loops, and every action is recorded for replay and audit.

def run_suite(agent, tasks, env_factory, k=3):
    rows = []
    for task in tasks:                          # your real tasks           #@1
        outcomes = []
        for _ in range(k):                                                 #@4
            env = env_factory(task.start_state)  # staging replica          #@2
            agent.run(task.instruction, env, max_steps=task.budget)
            outcomes.append(task.check(env))     # outcome, not clicks      #@3
        rows.append({"adversarial": task.adversarial,                      #@5
                     "passes": sum(outcomes)})
    normal = [r for r in rows if not r["adversarial"]]
    return {"pass@1": mean(r["passes"] / k for r in normal),
            f"pass^{k}": mean(r["passes"] == k for r in normal),          #@4
            "injection_fooled": mean(r["passes"] < k                        #@5
                                     for r in rows if r["adversarial"])}

import jiwer
from collections import defaultdict
from kavach.speech import load_turns, identify_language, RECOGNISERS, say   # your wrappers
from kavach.amounts import words_to_rupees, rupees_in_words                  # your rules

TURNS = load_turns("calls/2026-08/", sample_rate=8000)   # human-transcribed  #@1
PHRASES = ["Kavach Suraksha Plus", "nominee", "grace period",               #@4
           "lapse", "revival", "rider", "premium", "surrender value"]        #@4

def transcribe(turn):
    lang = identify_language(turn.audio)          # every turn, not once a call  #@2
    asr = RECOGNISERS[lang]                       # Indic-tuned, 8 kHz adapted   #@3
    hyp = asr.transcribe(turn.audio, language=lang, phrases=PHRASES)     #@3,4
    return lang, hyp

def evaluate(turns):
    pairs, amt = defaultdict(list), [0, 0]
    for t in turns:
        lang, hyp = transcribe(t)
        pairs[t.lang].append((t.reference, hyp.text))    # true language slice  #@6
        if t.amount is not None:                                             #@5
            amt[0] += words_to_rupees(hyp.text) == t.amount   # "saadhe teen hazaar"  #@5
            amt[1] += 1
    for lang, p in sorted(pairs.items()):
        refs, hyps = map(list, zip(*p))
        print(lang, f"WER {jiwer.wer(refs, hyps):.1%}", f"CER {jiwer.cer(refs, hyps):.1%}")  #@6
    print(f"amounts right {amt[0] / amt[1]:.1%}")                          #@6

def confirm_amount(hyp, lang):                                               #@5
    value = words_to_rupees(hyp.text)                                        #@5
    if value is None or hyp.confidence < 0.8:                                #@6
        return None                                   # ask again, then a person  #@6
    say(f"{rupees_in_words(value, lang)}, sahi hai?", lang=lang)  # read it back  #@5
    return value
steps: Test on your own calls

Kavach Bima, a fictional insurer, samples turns from its own recorded calls, at the 8 kHz the phone line delivers, and has people transcribe them. The sample is stratified: 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali, 10% English. A clean wideband benchmark would flatter every vendor.
Identify the language on every turn

Callers switch. A policyholder opens in Tamil, then says the policy number in English. With the language fixed per call, Hinglish WER rose from 18% to 24% even on the Indic-tuned model, and Tamil, Bengali and English got worse too.
Route to a recogniser tuned for it

Each language goes to a recogniser trained on Indian speech and adapted to 8 kHz audio. The English-first model got 66% of Tamil words wrong; the Indic-tuned one with telephony tuning and per-turn language ID gets 17%, and 16% with the vocabulary added.
Boost your own words

Plan names and policy terms, such as “Kavach Suraksha Plus”, “grace period” and “revival”, are passed as phrase hints so the recogniser prefers them. They are rare in general speech, so without hints they come out as similar-sounding everyday words.
Turn amounts into numbers, then read them back

“saadhe teen hazaar” is 3.5 × 1,000 = ₹3,500; “dhai lakh” is ₹2,50,000; “paune chaar hazaar” is ₹3,750. Rules turn the words into a value, and the agent reads it back in the caller’s language before acting. Amount capture rose from 55% to 91%.
Score per language, not one average

WER and CER are printed per true language, so a good Hindi score cannot hide Tamil. Blended WER fell from 41% to 12%, and calls needing a person from 55% to 17%. Low-confidence amounts are asked again, then handed to a person.

from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket
app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/incoming")                       # provider webhook on a call  #@1
def incoming():
    return twiml_connect_stream(url="wss://voice.dhanseva.in/media")     #@1

@app.websocket("/media")                                                 #@2
async def media(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    call = VoiceSession(stt=indic_stt, llm=agent, tts=hindi_tts,         #@2
                        sample_rate=8000, codec="mulaw")                  #@2
    async for msg in ws.iter_json():
        if msg["event"] == "media":
            await call.feed(msg["media"]["payload"])
        elif msg["event"] == "dtmf":                                     #@3
            await call.on_keypress(msg["dtmf"]["digit"])                  #@3
        if call.wants_human:                                              #@4
            summary = call.summary()          # intent, loan id, verified  #@4
            await transfer_warm(call.sid, queue="loans", note=summary)    #@4
            break
    crm.log_call(call.sid, call.transcript, consent=call.recording_ok)    #@5
# media region: Mumbai; outbound: DND scrub + approved number series     #@6
steps: Answer the call
Dhan Seva, a fictional NBFC, points its provider’s webhook at /incoming, which tells the provider to stream the call audio to the agent.
Stream the audio
Audio arrives as 8 kHz μ-law frames over a WebSocket; the session runs speech-to-text, the agent and Hindi text-to-speech on the stream.
Handle the keypad
Callers can still press keys: DTMF digits reach the agent, useful for entering a loan number or choosing a language.
Transfer warm
When the caller wants a person or the agent is unsure, it hands the call to the loans queue with a summary: intent, loan id and whether the caller was verified.
Log and record with consent
Every call is logged to the CRM with its transcript; recording happens only after the consent notice.
Keep media near callers
With media in a Mumbai region, replies start in about 700 ms instead of 950 ms. Outbound calls are scrubbed against DND preferences and use the approved number series.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
TOOLS = [{"type": "computer_toolset_20260801"}]

def run_task(task: str, vm, max_steps: int = 40):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=2048,
            tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            output = vm.execute(block.name, block.input)       # click, type, zoom...
            shot = vm.screenshot(max_long_edge=1568)           # resize before returning
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": [output, shot]})
        if not results:
            return messages                                    # task finished
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise TimeoutError("step budget exhausted; hand to a person")

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

ALLOWED = ("www.nseindia.com", "www.bseindia.com")

def todays_notices(llm, company: str):
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        browser = p.chromium.launch()
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto("https://www.bseindia.com/corporates/ann.html")   # scripted step
        page.get_by_role("textbox", name="Security Name").fill(company)
        page.get_by_role("button", name="Submit").click()

        tree = page.locator("body").aria_snapshot()                # ~3k tokens
        choice = llm.pick_link(tree, goal=f"today's corporate actions for {company}")
        link = page.get_by_role("link", name=choice.name)
        assert link.get_attribute("href").split("/")[2] in ALLOWED, "off-allowlist"
        link.click()

        summary = llm.extract(page.locator("main").aria_snapshot(),
                              schema=CorporateAction)               # structured output
        browser.close()
        return summary

            "Never read out full card or account numbers. If you are not sure "
            "what the caller said, ask once, then transfer to a person."))

    session = AgentSession(
        stt=sarvam.STT(language="hi-IN"),        # tested on real phone audio
        llm=openai.LLM(model="gpt-4.1-mini"),    # a fast model; example name
        tts=sarvam.TTS(target_language_code="hi-IN"),
        vad=silero.VAD.load(),
        turn_detection=MultilingualModel())      # smarter than silence alone

import statistics

def run_suite(agent, tasks, env_factory, k=3):
    rows = []
    for task in tasks:                                   # real tasks + adversarial ones
        outcomes = []
        for _ in range(k):
            env = env_factory(task.start_state)          # fresh staging replica
            agent.run(task.instruction, env, max_steps=task.budget)
            outcomes.append(task.check(env))             # outcome, not clicks
        rows.append({"task": task.id, "adversarial": task.adversarial,
                     "passes": sum(outcomes), "k": k})
    normal = [r for r in rows if not r["adversarial"]]
    return {
        "pass@1": statistics.mean(r["passes"] / k for r in normal),
        f"pass^{k}": statistics.mean(r["passes"] == k for r in normal),
        "injection_fooled": statistics.mean(
            r["passes"] < k for r in rows if r["adversarial"]),
    }
agenteval.note: Report the interval as well as the mean, and re-run the suite whenever the model, prompt or target application changes.

from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/media")
async def media(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    frames = 0
    async for raw in ws.iter_text():
        msg = json.loads(raw)

            print("call", msg["start"]["callSid"])
        elif msg["event"] == "media":
            audio = base64.b64decode(msg["media"]["payload"])   # 8 kHz mu-law, 20 ms

            print("frames:", frames, "seconds:", frames * 0.02)

voice.title: Speaking the reply
voice.code:
async def respond(text_stream, tts, call):
    reply = "".join([chunk async for chunk in text_stream])
    audio = await tts.synthesize(reply)
    await call.play(audio)
voice.explain: The whole reply is collected before any audio is made, so the caller waits for the model to finish and for synthesis of every word. Stream sentence by sentence so the first words play within a couple of hundred milliseconds.

also.4: Playing audio is fine; the delay comes from waiting for the full text.

multimodal.title: Cross-checking an amount
multimodal.code:
def amounts_match(vision_value, ocr_text):
    return str(vision_value) in ocr_text
multimodal.explain: A raw substring check fails on “18,450”, “₹18,450.00” or Devanagari digits, creating false disagreements, and passes wrongly when 450 happens to appear inside another number. Normalise both sides and compare whole numbers.
multimodal.fix: return any(to_number(t) == float(vision_value) for t in numbers_in(normalise_digits(ocr_text)))

actsafe.title: The domain allowlist

agenteval.title: Reporting reliability
agenteval.explain: This averages all runs, which is pass@1 again, not reliability. pass^k is the share of tasks that pass on every one of their k runs.
agenteval.fix: return sum(all(t["runs"][:k]) for t in results) / len(results)

also.2: Collecting the first k runs per task is fine.

Reading the amount back for confirmation
Normalisation, vocabulary and read-back all work on amounts. A blended WER measures nothing about them.
Hospital helpline recordings are used to evaluate speech models. Which practices fit the DPDP Act and good hygiene? Choose all that apply.
Tell callers about recording and its purpose
Redact names, phone and policy numbers from transcripts used for scoring
Keep recordings forever in case they are useful
Restrict who can listen to raw audio
Recordings are personal data: give notice, minimise, redact and restrict access. Keeping them indefinitely is not good practice. Educational framing, not legal advice.
An Indic-tuned stack costs ₹0.90 a minute more than an English-first one. Which effects can still make it cheaper overall? Choose all that apply.
Fewer repeated questions and shorter calls
Fewer wrong amounts to correct later
People cost far more per minute than speech models, so accuracy that avoids handovers, repeats and corrections pays for the premium. Higher WER does the opposite.

gui.q: How does a computer-use agent work, end to end?
gui.model: The model is given a computer-use tool. Each turn it sees the latest screenshot and returns an action such as a click at coordinates or typing text. Your harness executes the action in a VM, scaling coordinates to the real screen, then returns a new screenshot so the model can check the result. The loop runs until the model stops requesting actions or a step budget is reached, when a person takes over.

gui.q: Why do GUI agents struggle with long tasks, and what helps?
gui.model: Small per-step error rates compound: 97% per step over 18 steps is under 60%. Downscaled screenshots hide small text, and without checking after each action the agent continues from a wrong state. Verification after actions, zooming into small regions, accessibility data where available, sensible step budgets and splitting long tasks all raise end-to-end success.

gui.q: When should you not use a GUI agent?
gui.model: When there is an API or an accessible web interface, use it: it is faster, cheaper and more reliable. GUI agents also fit poorly with high-volume or latency-sensitive work. They are a bridge for legacy systems, run in a sandbox with checks, until an integration exists.

browser.q: How should a browser agent observe a page?
browser.model: Default to the accessibility tree, which lists roles, names and stable element references in a few thousand tokens. Add screenshots when layout or visuals matter, such as charts. Avoid raw HTML, which is large and noisy and wastes context on markup and scripts.

browser.q: Design a reliable agent that collects documents from several portals every day.
browser.model: Use a controlled browser such as Playwright with a clean profile. Script the fixed route of navigation, search and downloads, and use the agent only for judgement, such as finding today’s notice, reading accessibility snapshots. Restrict navigation to an allowlist, extract into a schema and validate it, record sessions, and alert when a script step fails because a site changed.

browser.q: What do WebArena scores tell you about a browser agent?
browser.model: WebArena runs 812 tasks on self-hosted sites such as shops, forums and GitLab, with functional checks; the top reported score in mid-2026 was about 74% against roughly 78% for people. It measures general capability, not success on your portals, logins or pop-ups, so evaluate on your own sites.

voice.q: Break down the latency of a voice agent and how you would reduce it.
voice.model: Measure from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio. The budget is roughly network 30–80 ms, end-of-turn detection 150–300 ms, speech-to-text finalisation, LLM first token 150–400 ms and synthesis first audio 100–200 ms, for about 600–800 ms. Reduce it by streaming every stage, using a turn-detection model instead of long silence waits, choosing a fast model for the first reply, and keeping services close to the telephony provider.

voice.q: What is different about building voice agents for Indian callers?
voice.model: Callers mix Hindi and English, switch mid-sentence and often call over narrowband phone lines. Recognition is much better for Hindi than for lower-resource languages such as Bhojpuri and Maithili, where error rates can be several times higher. Evaluate speech models on real calls per language, handle code-mixed text, and route callers to a person when confidence is low.

Speech-to-speech models can reply faster and handle interruptions naturally, but give less control over recognition, language coverage and logging. A cascaded pipeline lets you pick India-tuned recognition, inspect transcripts and swap components, at the cost of more latency to manage. Choose by measured latency and accuracy on your callers’ languages.

multimodal.q: How would you build a pipeline that reads claim documents from phone photos?
multimodal.model: Preprocess each photo by deskewing, cropping and resizing to the model’s limit. Extract fields into a strict schema with a vision model, validate formats, and cross-check critical fields such as amounts and dates with a second reader such as OCR. Route disagreements to an assessor, keep the original image for audit, and mask personal data in logs.

multimodal.q: Why do image size and preprocessing matter for vision models?
multimodal.model: APIs downscale large images to a maximum size, so small text can become unreadable; very small images lose detail. Crop to the document, straighten it, resize deliberately to the limit, and tile or zoom into regions with small text, accepting the extra cost where accuracy matters.

multimodal.q: How do you handle handwriting in regional scripts?
multimodal.model: Expect lower accuracy and measure it separately for each script and document type. Cross-check with a second reader, set review thresholds per segment, and keep a person in the loop for handwritten documents until results justify more automation.

actsafe.q: What safeguards would you require before a browser agent can click buttons that move money?
actsafe.model: Run it in an isolated browser or VM with no personal data, restrict it to an allowlist of domains, fill credentials from a vault so the model never sees them, treat on-screen text as data and screen it for injection, require human confirmation of payments, reversals and submissions, cap steps and spend, and record every session for replay.

actsafe.q: How can a web page hijack a computer-use agent?
actsafe.model: Text on a page, in a banner, a comment or hidden in the markup, can read like an instruction, such as “click Confirm Reversal”. If the agent treats it as a command it acts for the attacker. Mitigate by treating screen content as untrusted data, screening for injection, restricting domains and confirming irreversible actions, so a successful injection still cannot cause harm alone.

actsafe.q: Why not confirm every action to be safe?
actsafe.model: Frequent prompts train people to approve without looking, which removes the safety they were meant to add. Confirm only irreversible or high-impact actions, show enough context to decide, and rely on the other layers for the rest.

agenteval.q: A vendor quotes a top OSWorld score. How do you decide whether to deploy its agent?
agenteval.model: Treat the score as evidence of general capability on fixed tasks, often self-reported with the vendor’s scaffolding. Build an evaluation from your own tasks in a staging replica, check outcomes rather than clicks, run each task several times and report pass^k, and include injected pages and irreversible actions. Launch read-only tasks first.

agenteval.q: What is pass^k and why does it matter for agents?
agenteval.model: pass^k is the share of tasks an agent passes on every one of k repeated runs. Agents are not fully consistent, so pass^k is lower than single-run success, and it is closer to what customers experience when they rely on the agent repeatedly.

agenteval.q: How would you evaluate a voice agent before launch?
agenteval.model: Use recorded real calls, with consent, covering each language, accent and channel. Measure word error rate per language, latency from end of speech to first audio, task completion and transfers to people, and review failures by segment before widening the rollout.

indicspeech.q: How would you evaluate and choose speech recognition for a helpline serving Hindi, Hinglish, Tamil, Bengali and English callers?
indicspeech.model: Sample and transcribe your own calls at the phone line’s 8 kHz, stratified by language, accent and code-mixing. Score each candidate, English-first, multilingual general and Indic-tuned, on WER and CER per language, and on what matters for the business: amounts, policy numbers and names. Add per-turn language identification, custom vocabulary and amount rules, test again, and weigh accuracy against cost per minute including the people who take handed-over calls.

indicspeech.q: Calls are 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali and 10% English, with WERs of 30%, 51%, 66%, 60% and 15%. What is the blended WER, and what does it hide? Show the working.
indicspeech.model: 0.45 × 30 + 0.20 × 51 + 0.15 × 66 + 0.10 × 60 + 0.10 × 15 = 13.5 + 10.2 + 9.9 + 6.0 + 1.5 = 41.1%. It hides that Tamil callers lose two words in three and Bengali callers three in five, while English looks fine at 15%. Report every slice and fix the worst first.

indicspeech.q: A caller says “saadhe teen hazaar” and the system records ₹3,000. Another says “dhai lakh” and gets nothing. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
indicspeech.model: The transcript was probably right but the conversion was not: the rules ignored saadhe (add a half) and did not know dhai (2.5), so ₹3,500 became ₹3,000 and ₹2,50,000 was dropped. Add inverse text normalisation rules for Hindi fractions and Indian scales (sau, hazaar, lakh, crore), boost number words with custom vocabulary, read the value back in the caller’s language before acting, and track amount accuracy as its own metric on your calls.

telephony.q: How would you put a voice agent on a bank’s helpline?
telephony.model: Connect through a telephony provider or SIP trunk with media processed near callers, stream audio to the agent and handle DTMF and hold, transfer warm with a summary into the contact centre, log to the CRM, record with consent and follow TRAI rules for outbound calls.

cases.title: The helpline that must also do the back-office work
cases.brief: Sangam Bank wants a voice agent to handle about 1.2 lakh calls a month on card blocking and UPI dispute status, in Hindi and Hinglish. A vendor proposes pairing it with a GUI agent that looks up dispute status in a legacy desktop application with no API. The dispute screens include a reversal button. You are asked which techniques matter before launch, and in what order.
evidence: In testing, the GUI agent clicked “Confirm reversal” after a banner on the screen told it to. It runs with the same access a desk officer has.
The pilot voice agent replies about 1.9 seconds after callers finish speaking, and 16% of callers hang up.
A general speech model misheard about one word in five on Hinglish phone calls, and about 15% of callers - mostly from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh - speak Bhojpuri or Maithili.
The vendor cites an 85% OSWorld-Verified score for its GUI agent. There is no test of the bank's own screens.
Some customers send photos of UPI receipts over WhatsApp as proof of payment.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.actsafe: Start here. A GUI agent reversed a transaction because text on the screen told it to, and it holds a desk officer's full access - that is on-screen text acting as instructions, which is the named pitfall, on a screen with a reversal button. Treat everything rendered as data and never as instruction, run the agent in an isolated session rather than a person's own desktop, strip its permissions to read-only for status lookups, and keep confirmations rare enough that nobody approves blindly.
why.voice: 1.9 seconds after the caller stops speaking is why 16% hang up: the budget for a natural reply is far tighter, and silence-based turn detection waiting 800 ms is usually a large part of it. Write the per-stage budget down - turn detection, transcription, model, speech synthesis - and fix the stage that dominates rather than the one that is easiest.
why.indicspeech: One word in five wrong on Hinglish phone calls makes everything downstream guesswork, and the 15% speaking Bhojpuri or Maithili will be worse. Choose the speech vendor on your own recorded calls rather than a clean benchmark, report word error rate per language instead of one blended figure, allow the language to change mid-call because callers switch, and provide a human fallback for the languages you cannot serve.
why.agenteval: An 85% OSWorld-Verified score is a score on somebody else's screens, and the bank has tested none of its own. Build a task set from the bank's real workflows, run each task several times because these agents are not deterministic, test against live screens rather than static snapshots, and re-run after every model update.
why.gui: Useful, and the honest framing is that it is a bridge: the legacy application has no API, so screen driving is the only route today. Keep a verification step at the end of every task, and treat the lack of an API as a project with a deadline rather than a permanent condition.
why.multimodal: Useful: WhatsApp receipt photos need reading, and the cautions matter here - do not send huge images the API will downscale anyway, never trust a single read for an amount or an identifier, and include handwriting and regional scripts in the evaluation set.
why.telephony: Useful and worth checking early: if media is routed through a distant region it adds a quarter-second to every turn before the agent has thought at all, which comes straight out of the budget you are about to write.
why.browser: Not needed: the back-office system is a legacy desktop application, not a web portal. Browser automation would be the answer if this were a vendor website.

firstWhy.voice: The reason the pilot is failing commercially - 16% of callers hanging up is the number that decides whether this launches - and it is your second step. But a slow helpline loses calls you can win back, while a GUI agent that reverses a transaction because a banner asked it to moves money that nobody authorised. One is recoverable.
firstWhy.indicspeech: The deepest quality problem here: one word in five wrong makes every later stage a guess, and the Bhojpuri and Maithili slice is being ignored entirely. Still second-tier in ordering, because it degrades answers rather than taking actions - and because the agent with the reversal button is the one shipping alongside it.
firstWhy.agenteval: Exactly the right scepticism about the vendor's 85%, and you cannot launch without your own task set. But evaluation tells you how often the agent succeeds; it does not stop the failure mode you have already observed, which needs a permission change rather than a measurement.

cases.model: Start with safety for agents that act on screens, because the GUI agent has already reversed a transaction on the instruction of a banner and it runs with a desk officer's full access: treat on-screen text as data and never as instruction, isolate the session from any human desktop, reduce its permissions to read-only for status lookups so a reversal is not reachable at all, and keep confirmations rare enough to be read. Then fix the voice loop, since 1.9 seconds of silence after a caller finishes is why 16% hang up - write a per-stage latency budget covering turn detection, transcription, model and synthesis, and attack whichever stage dominates rather than the easiest one. Next choose speech on the bank's own recorded calls rather than a clean benchmark, report word error rate per language instead of one blended number, let the language switch mid-call, and arrange a human fallback for Bhojpuri and Maithili. Then build your own evaluation: real bank workflows, several runs per task because these agents are not deterministic, live screens rather than snapshots, and a re-run after every model update - the vendor's 85% is a score on other people's software. Keep the GUI agent as an explicit bridge until an API exists, read WhatsApp receipts with care over amounts, and check where telephony media is being routed. Browser automation does not apply to a desktop application.
cases.note: The commercially urgent number was the 16% hang-up rate and it still came second, because the other agent in this system can move money on the instruction of a banner. Case 3 has no screens at all, and the whole answer shifts to the phone line.

actsafe: Symptom 1: the GUI agent clicked “Confirm reversal” because a banner on the screen told it to, and it runs with a desk officer's full access. What did the agent treat as an instruction, and what should it have been?
Anything rendered on a screen is content, and content can be written by someone else. Think about where the agent runs, what it is permitted to do, and how often it asks before acting.

Safety for Agents that Act on Screens. All three pitfalls are here: running in someone's everyday environment, letting on-screen text act as instructions, and confirmation prompts so frequent people approve blindly.
voice: Symptom 2: the agent replies about 1.9 seconds after the caller stops speaking, and 16% of callers hang up. What is the budget for a reply that feels like a conversation, and which stage usually eats it?
Break the turn into stages and give each one a number. One of them is often waiting for silence, and the default threshold is longer than you would guess.
Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets. Read the pitfall about silence-based turn detection waiting 800 ms.
indicspeech: Symptom 3: one word in five wrong on Hinglish phone calls, and 15% of callers speaking Bhojpuri or Maithili. What was the speech model chosen on, and what is a single accuracy number hiding?
Clean benchmark audio is nothing like a phone line, and one blended figure can hide an entire failing language. Also ask what happens when a caller switches language halfway through.
Speech in Indian Languages. All three pitfalls apply: a clean wideband benchmark, one blended error rate hiding a failing slice, and fixing the language at the start of the call.
agenteval: Symptom 4: the vendor cites 85% on OSWorld-Verified, and nobody has tested the bank's own screens. What does that 85% actually measure?
Somebody else's tasks on somebody else's software. What you need is your own task set - and there are specific things to get right about how many times you run each one and what you run it against.
Evaluating Computer-Use Agents. Read all three pitfalls: a public benchmark treated as your success rate, static page snapshots, and one run per task.

drop.browser: Browser automation drives web portals that have no API. What kind of application does the dispute status live in?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right, and the number that will decide the launch is the hang-up rate. Before ordering by that, ask what each failure costs if it happens once more - and note that one of these agents has a reversal button within reach.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 16% of callers hang up because the agent takes 1.9 seconds to reply, which is the number deciding whether this launches at all.
One word in five is misheard on Hinglish calls, so everything downstream of transcription is guesswork.
A GUI agent with a desk officer's access has already reversed a transaction because a banner told it to.
whyFirst.why: Order by what cannot be taken back. The hang-up rate is the commercial problem and the transcription error rate is the deepest quality problem, and both are on the list - but a dropped call can be made again, and a misheard word produces a wrong answer somebody will question. An unauthorised reversal has already happened once in testing, on an agent holding full desk access, and nothing else on this list prevents the next one.

cases.title: The filings agent that logs in as a person
cases.brief: An asset manager runs an agent each morning to collect filings, circulars and statements from fourteen regulator and exchange portals that have no APIs. It downloads and files them; it submits nothing, approves nothing and moves no money. Nobody speaks to it. The complaints are that it breaks whenever a portal changes, and that it has rather too much access to the engineer who built it.
evidence: The agent feeds raw HTML to the model, which fills the context and causes it to misread tables on the denser pages.
It runs in an engineer's everyday Chrome profile, signed into the firm's real portal accounts and that engineer's personal mail.
The workflow is fixed and identical every morning, yet it runs as a fully autonomous agent that re-discovers the navigation each time and breaks when a portal renames a label.
Testing is one run per task against saved page snapshots, and a vendor benchmark score was accepted as the expected success rate.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.browser: Start here, because three of the four symptoms are this technique's own pitfalls in order. Feeding raw HTML to the model is the first - extract the structure you need instead, or render and look at the page. Running a fully autonomous agent over a fixed daily workflow is the second - script what is stable and let the agent handle only what varies, which is also why a renamed label breaks the whole run today. And logging into real accounts from the agent's own browser profile is the third, which is symptom 2.
why.actsafe: The profile is the other half of symptom 2 and the reason it matters: an agent running in a person's everyday browser inherits every session that person has, including their personal mail. Give it a dedicated, isolated profile with only the portal credentials it needs. And since it reads untrusted web pages all morning, treat page text as data rather than instruction - the agent downloads today, but the same reasoning path would obey a page tomorrow if anyone gave it a submit button.
why.agenteval: One run per task against saved snapshots, with a vendor's benchmark accepted as the success rate, is three pitfalls at once. Portals change - that is the actual failure mode here - so test against live pages, run each task several times because these agents are not deterministic, and build your own task set rather than importing a score from someone else's.
why.gui: Useful as a comparison: driving a screen is the fallback when a page cannot be read reliably, and some portals may need it. Keep the end-of-task verification step either way - checking the right document actually arrived is cheap and catches a silent failure.
why.multimodal: Useful, and the right tool for the dense pages: looking at a rendered page beats parsing its HTML when layout carries the meaning, and some filings arrive as scans. Do not send oversized images, and include regional scripts in the evaluation.
why.voice: Not needed: nobody speaks to this agent and it makes no calls.
why.indicspeech: Not needed: there is no audio anywhere in this system.
why.telephony: Not needed: no phone lines, no contact centre, no transfers.

firstWhy.actsafe: A strong case, and your second step - an agent in the engineer's everyday profile has their personal mail session, which is indefensible. But this agent only reads and downloads: it submits nothing and moves no money, so the exposure is credential breadth rather than an irreversible action. Meanwhile three of the four symptoms are fixed by changing how it reads and how much of it is scripted.
firstWhy.agenteval: The sharpest reading of why it keeps breaking - snapshots cannot catch a portal that changed, and one run per task tells you nothing about a non-deterministic agent. But testing would reveal the breakage rather than remove it, and the cause is a fixed workflow being re-discovered every morning.
firstWhy.gui: Reasonable for the densest pages, and worth keeping in reserve. But these are web portals, so the question is first how the page is read and what is scripted - screen driving is the fallback, not the starting point.

cases.model: Start with browser automation, because three of the four symptoms are its documented pitfalls: raw HTML is being fed to the model and filling the context, so extract the structure you need or read a rendered page instead; a fixed daily workflow is being run by a fully autonomous agent, so script the stable navigation and let the model handle only what varies - which is why a renamed label currently breaks the whole run; and the agent is logging into real accounts from a human's browser profile. Then take that last point seriously as a safety matter: give the agent an isolated profile holding only the portal credentials it needs, nowhere near the engineer's personal sessions, and treat page text as data rather than instruction, since it reads untrusted pages all morning and the same reasoning would obey one the day someone grants it a submit button. Then build real evaluation: your own task set over the fourteen portals, run against live pages rather than snapshots because changing pages is the actual failure mode, several runs per task since the agent is not deterministic, and no borrowed benchmark as a success rate. Use a rendered-page read for the densest filings, and keep screen driving as a fallback with an end-of-task check that the right document arrived. Nothing here involves voice, Indian-language speech or telephony.
cases.note: Safety came second here and first in Case 1, for one reason: this agent only reads, while that one had a reversal button. The same shared-profile mistake is serious in both, but what it could do differed.

browser: Read symptoms 1, 2 and 3 together: raw HTML fed to the model, an everyday Chrome profile signed into real accounts, and a fixed daily workflow run by a fully autonomous agent that breaks on a renamed label. Three faults, one technique's guidance.
The question is whether the agent should read the page or look at it, how much of a stable workflow should be code rather than judgement, and whose browser session it is using.

Browser Automation Agents. All three pitfalls are in this evidence in order: raw HTML, fully autonomous agents for fixed workflows, and logging into real accounts from the agent's own browser profile.
actsafe: Symptom 2 again, from the other side: the agent is in a profile that is also signed into the engineer's personal mail. And it spends every morning reading pages written by other people. What two risks is that?
One is how much it can reach if anything goes wrong. The other is what happens when text it reads starts to look like an instruction.
Safety for Agents that Act on Screens. Read the pitfalls about running in someone's everyday browser and about letting on-screen text act as instructions.
agenteval: Symptom 4: one run per task, against saved page snapshots, with a vendor benchmark taken as the expected success rate. Now recall what actually breaks this agent - a portal changing a label. What would the current testing never catch?
Snapshots freeze the thing that moves. And a non-deterministic agent run once tells you about that run. Note what the vendor's number is a measurement of.
Evaluating Computer-Use Agents. All three pitfalls apply: a public benchmark as your success rate, static snapshots, and one run per task.

drop.voice: Realtime voice agents answer people speaking. Who speaks to this agent?
drop.indicspeech: Speech in Indian languages is about hearing callers correctly. What audio does this system process?
drop.telephony: Telephony integration connects a voice agent to phone lines and a contact centre. Which phone line is involved here?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. One of them owns three of the four symptoms outright - read its pitfalls against the evidence line by line before deciding the order.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The agent runs in an engineer's everyday browser profile, inheriting their personal mail session alongside the firm's portal accounts.
Raw HTML, an autonomous agent on a fixed workflow, and a shared browser profile are three pitfalls of one technique, and they cause the breakage being complained about.
Snapshots and single runs mean the testing could never detect a portal changing, which is the actual failure mode.
whyFirst.why: Order by what explains the complaints. The shared profile is serious and is your second step - but this agent only downloads, so the risk is credential breadth rather than an unauthorised action. The testing gap explains why breakage is a surprise rather than why it happens. What happens is that a stable daily workflow is being re-derived from raw HTML every morning, and that one technique's guidance addresses three of the four symptoms.

cases.title: The campaign that called people it should not have, through Virginia
cases.brief: An NBFC runs outbound reminder and collections calls with a voice agent across Hindi, Tamil and English, and escalates to human agents when a borrower disputes an amount. There are no screens, no browsers and no documents in the flow - only phone calls. A regulator notice has arrived, and the contact-centre head says transfers are making things worse rather than better.
evidence: Media for every call is routed through a US region, adding roughly a quarter of a second to each turn before the agent has begun thinking.
Escalations are cold transfers: the human agent receives no context and the borrower repeats everything. 31% of transfers end in a second complaint.
An outbound reminder campaign dialled numbers on the DND register, and a regulator notice followed.

Speech recognition was chosen on a clean wideband benchmark. On real calls, one blended error rate hides a failing Tamil slice, and callers switch language mid-call while the agent fixes it at call start.
Turn detection is silence-based with an 800 ms threshold, so the agent talks over borrowers who pause mid-sentence and waits through those who have finished.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.telephony: Start here, because three symptoms are this layer and one of them has a regulator attached. Dialling numbers on the DND register is the pitfall with legal consequences - stop the campaign and fix the suppression list first. Then bring media routing into the region, since a quarter-second added to every turn is spent before the agent thinks at all and comes straight out of the latency budget. And replace cold transfers with warm ones carrying the transcript and the borrower's intent, because 31% of transfers producing a second complaint is a handover problem rather than an agent problem.
why.voice: An 800 ms silence threshold is the named pitfall and it explains both halves of symptom 5: the agent interrupts borrowers who pause mid-sentence and leaves dead air for those who have finished. Move to a model-based turn detector and write the per-stage budget - turn detection, transcription, model, synthesis - knowing that routing has already taken 250 ms of it.
why.indicspeech: Speech chosen on clean wideband audio does not survive a phone line, and one blended error rate hiding a failing Tamil slice is exactly the pitfall named - on collections calls, where amounts and dates must be heard correctly. Benchmark vendors on your own recorded calls, report per language, let the language switch mid-call rather than fixing it at the start, and keep a human fallback for the languages you cannot serve well.
why.agenteval: Useful and currently missing: an evaluation set built from real recorded calls, scored per language, run repeatedly, and re-run after every model or vendor change. It is how you would have caught the Tamil slice before a customer did.
why.multimodal: Useful if borrowers start sending payment screenshots to support a dispute, which is a natural next step - but nothing in this flow reads an image today.
why.gui: Not needed: there are no screens in this system. The agent makes calls.
why.browser: Not needed: no portals and no web pages anywhere in the flow.
why.actsafe: Not needed, and worth stating because it was the first move in Case 1: this agent controls no screen and clicks nothing, so there is no on-screen instruction to be deceived by and no unauthorised action it can take through a UI. Its risks are regulatory and conversational instead.

firstWhy.voice: The most visible conversational fault - an 800 ms threshold makes the agent both interrupt and stall - and your second step. But 250 ms of your budget is already being lost to routing before the agent thinks, so fixing turn detection while the media still crosses an ocean is optimising inside a smaller budget than you need to have.
firstWhy.indicspeech: The deepest quality problem, and on collections calls mishearing an amount is serious. Still second-tier in ordering: a failing Tamil slice produces wrong conversations, while an outbound campaign dialling DND numbers has already produced a regulator notice, and that one is not a quality issue at all.
firstWhy.agenteval: Right that none of this is being measured per language on real calls, and it is how the Tamil slice would have surfaced earlier. But measurement follows the fixes here, and the item with a regulator behind it does not wait for a test suite.

cases.model: Start with the telephony layer, because three symptoms live there and one of them is a legal matter: stop the outbound campaign dialling DND-registered numbers and fix the suppression list before anything else. Bring media routing into the region, since a quarter-second added to every turn is consumed before the agent begins to think and is simply taken out of your latency budget. Replace cold transfers with warm ones carrying the transcript and the borrower's stated intent, because 31% of transfers ending in a second complaint is a handover failure rather than an agent failure. Then fix the voice loop: move off an 800 ms silence threshold, which makes the agent interrupt borrowers who pause and stall for those who have finished, and write the per-stage budget with the routing saving in hand. Next choose speech on your own recorded calls rather than clean wideband audio, report word error rate per language instead of one blended figure that hides Tamil, allow the language to change mid-call since borrowers switch, and keep a human fallback where accuracy is not good enough - these are collections calls, and amounts and dates must be heard right. Build an evaluation set from real calls, scored per language and re-run after every change. There are no screens, pages or documents here, so GUI, browser and screen-safety techniques do not apply.
cases.note: Screen safety was the first move in Case 1 and does not apply at all here, because this agent has no hands. Three cases, three different first moves - the reversal button, the way a page is read, the phone line - and each time the hardest-to-undo failure was somewhere other than the model.

telephony: Symptoms 1, 2 and 3 are all below the agent: media routed through a US region costing a quarter-second per turn, cold transfers where the borrower repeats everything, and a campaign that dialled DND-registered numbers. What layer is that?
How the voice agent plugs into real phone lines and a contact centre - routing, handovers to humans, and the rules about who may be called. One of the three has a regulator behind it.
Telephony and Contact-Centre Integration. All three pitfalls are in this evidence: media bouncing through a distant region, cold transfers, and outbound campaigns ignoring DND.
voice: Symptom 5: silence-based turn detection with an 800 ms threshold, so the agent talks over borrowers who pause mid-sentence and waits through those who have finished. What is wrong with deciding a turn has ended by measuring silence?
A pause is not the end of a sentence. The fix is a better way of detecting the turn - and a written budget for every stage, because you have already lost 250 ms elsewhere.
Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets. The first pitfall - silence-based turn detection that waits 800 ms - is symptom 5 exactly.
indicspeech: Symptom 4: speech chosen on a clean wideband benchmark, one blended error rate hiding a failing Tamil slice, and the language fixed at call start while borrowers switch mid-call. These are collections calls with amounts in them.
Three separate errors about hearing Indian languages on a phone line: what you chose the vendor on, how you report accuracy, and when you decide which language is being spoken.
Speech in Indian Languages. All three pitfalls are symptom 4 in order: a clean benchmark, one blended figure hiding a slice, and fixing the language at the start of the call.

drop.gui: Screen-understanding agents use applications the way a person does. Which application does this agent click?
drop.browser: Browser automation drives portals without APIs. Which web page is in this flow?
drop.actsafe: Screen-action safety stops an agent on a browser or desktop from doing damage - including being instructed by on-screen text. What does this agent control, and why does that make this the opposite of Case 1?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right, and the one with legal consequences is not about the agent's conversation at all. Look at which layer each symptom sits in: three of these five are below the model entirely.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: An outbound campaign dialled DND-registered numbers and a regulator notice has already arrived, and two more symptoms sit in the same layer.
An 800 ms silence threshold makes the agent interrupt and stall, which is the fault borrowers notice on every call.
One blended error rate is hiding a failing Tamil slice on calls where amounts and dates must be heard correctly.
whyFirst.why: Order by what you cannot undo and by what shares a fix. The turn detection is the most audible fault and the Tamil slice the deepest quality problem - but calls already placed to DND-registered numbers cannot be unplaced, and the notice is on the desk. The same layer also holds the 250 ms of routing you need back before a latency budget is worth writing, and the cold transfers producing a second complaint a third of the time.

gui.t: A GUI task takes 18 actions, and each succeeds independently with probability 0.97. What share of tasks succeed end to end, in percent?
gui.a: 0.97¹⁸ ≈ 0.578, or about 57.8%. At 0.995 per step it would be about 91.4%. Long tasks need very high per-step accuracy, which is why verifying after each action pays off.
iv: When would you use a GUI agent instead of an API?

Only when there is no API or accessible interface: legacy desktop apps, terminals, or portals you cannot integrate with. GUI agents are slower, costlier and less reliable than API calls, so they bridge a gap until an API exists, and they run in a sandboxed VM with verification and a human fallback.
Why do GUI agents fail on long tasks?

Errors compound: a small chance of a wrong click or misread field at each step multiplies over dozens of steps. Downscaled screenshots hide small text, and without checking the screen after each action the agent carries on from a wrong state. Verification, zoom, step budgets and shorter tasks all help.
mis: No check after each action
Take a screenshot and verify the expected change
Screenshots larger than the model’s limit
Resize first and scale coordinates back

browser.t: A browser agent reads 12 pages per task. Raw HTML costs about 25,000 tokens a page and an accessibility snapshot about 3,000. At ₹0.25 per 1,000 input tokens, how much does switching save per task, in ₹?
browser.a: 12 × (25,000 − 3,000) = 264,000 tokens; 264 × ₹0.25 = ₹66 saved per task. The snapshot is also easier for the model to act on, because it names roles and elements instead of burying them in markup.
iv: Screenshot, HTML or accessibility tree: which should a browser agent observe?

Usually the accessibility tree: it is compact, lists roles and names, and gives stable references to act on. Add screenshots where layout or visuals matter, such as charts or canvases. Raw HTML is complete but large and noisy, and wastes context.
Why script parts of a browser workflow instead of letting the agent do everything?

Steps that never change, such as navigation and login, are faster, cheaper and more reliable in code. Letting the agent handle only what varies, such as finding the right notice or reading its contents, reduces errors and cost and keeps the flow auditable.
mis: Raw HTML in the prompt
Use the accessibility snapshot
A fully autonomous agent for a fixed route
Script the fixed steps, use the agent for judgement

voice.t: A cascaded voice agent has network 60 ms, end-of-turn detection 250 ms, speech-to-text finalisation 120 ms, LLM first token 200 ms and speech synthesis first audio 150 ms. What is the total from the end of the caller’s speech to first audio, in ms?
voice.a: 60 + 250 + 120 + 200 + 150 = 780 ms, inside the acceptable 500–800 ms range. Waiting for 800 ms of silence instead of smart turn detection would add 550 ms and push it past 1.3 seconds.
iv: How do you get a voice agent under 800 ms?

Stream every stage so speech-to-text runs while the caller talks and synthesis starts on the first words of the reply; use smart turn detection rather than long silence timeouts; pick a fast model for the first response; keep servers close to the telephony provider; and consider speech-to-speech models where their language coverage is good enough.
What is different about voice agents for Indian customers?

Callers mix Hindi and English, switch languages mid-sentence and call over narrowband phone lines. Recognition is far better for Hindi than for Bhojpuri, Maithili and other lower-resource languages. Evaluate speech models on real calls in each language, handle code-mixed text, and route callers to a person when recognition confidence is low.
mis: Silence-based end-of-turn detection
Use a turn-detection model and allow barge-in
Choosing speech models on clean benchmarks
Test on real phone calls in each language

multimodal.t: A pipeline reads 10,000 claim documents a month. The vision model is wrong on 4% of key fields, and cross-checking with OCR catches 70% of those errors and sends them for review. How many documents a month still reach the system with a wrong key field?
multimodal.a: 10,000 × 4% = 400 wrong; 70% caught leaves 400 × 0.3 = 120 documents. The cross-check also sends correct documents to review when the two readers disagree, so tune it to keep that load manageable.
iv: How would you read KYC documents with a multimodal model safely?

Preprocess images by deskewing, cropping and resizing; extract into a strict schema; validate formats and checksums; cross-check critical fields with a second reader such as OCR; route disagreements to a person; mask identifiers in logs; and keep the original image for audit.
Why does image resolution matter for a vision model?

APIs downscale large images to a maximum size, so small text can become unreadable, and very low resolution loses detail. Resize deliberately to the model’s limit, crop to the document, and tile or zoom into regions with small text when needed, accepting the extra cost.
mis: Trusting a single read for amounts or IDs
Cross-check with a second reader
Sending raw phone photos
Deskew, crop and resize first

actsafe.t: Without safeguards, an agent takes a harmful action in 40 of 1,000 tasks. An allowlist removes 60% of those, injection screening halves what remains, and human confirmation of irreversible actions stops 90% of the rest. How many harmful actions remain per 1,000 tasks?
actsafe.a: 40 × 0.4 = 16; × 0.5 = 8; × 0.1 = 0.8 harmful actions per 1,000 tasks. Each layer fails sometimes, so their product is what keeps the rate low.
iv: How do you stop a browser agent from following instructions hidden in a web page?

Treat everything on screen as data, never as instructions; screen observations with injection classifiers; restrict the agent to an allowlist of domains; keep it away from sensitive data and credentials; and require human confirmation for irreversible actions, so a successful injection cannot move money or submit forms on its own.
Why not let a computer-use agent type passwords?

Anything the model sees can leak through its outputs, logs or a successful injection. A vault or the harness should fill credentials directly into the field so the model never sees them, and sessions should use dedicated accounts with the least privilege.
mis: Running the agent in a staff member’s browser
Use an isolated browser or VM with no personal data
Confirming every click
Confirm only irreversible actions so people stay attentive

agenteval.t: An agent completes 78% of tasks on a single run. If each run were independent with the same success rate, what share of tasks would pass on all three of three runs, in percent?
agenteval.a: 0.78³ ≈ 0.475, or about 47.5%. Real agents are more consistent than independent coin flips, so measured pass^3 is usually higher, such as 62%, but it is always below the single-run rate. Reliability needs repeated runs to measure.
iv: What do OSWorld and WebArena measure, and what don’t they?

OSWorld runs agents on real desktop and web tasks in virtual machines with script-based success checks; WebArena uses self-hosted websites such as shops, forums and GitLab. They measure general capability on fixed tasks. They do not reflect your applications, logins, latency, adversarial content or reliability over repeated runs, and many reported scores are self-reported with different scaffolding.
How would you evaluate a computer-use agent before launch?

Collect real tasks with outcome checks, run them in a staging replica rather than static snapshots, repeat each several times and report pass^k, include adversarial pages and irreversible actions, record sessions to analyse failures, and set launch criteria per task type, starting with read-only tasks.
mis: Taking a public benchmark score as your success rate
Evaluate on your own tasks and environment
One run per task
Repeat runs and report pass^k

indicspeech.t: Kavach Bima’s calls are 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali and 10% English. On its own 8 kHz calls, the Indic-tuned model’s word error rates are 10%, 14%, 16%, 14% and 11%. What is the blended WER, in percent?
indicspeech.a: 0.45 × 10 + 0.20 × 14 + 0.15 × 16 + 0.10 × 14 + 0.10 × 11 = 4.5 + 2.8 + 2.4 + 1.4 + 1.1 = 12.2%. The blend is a summary only: Tamil at 16% is a third worse than Hindi at 10%, so report every slice.
iv: How would you choose a speech-recognition model for an Indian-language helpline?

Sample and transcribe real calls at the channel’s 8 kHz, stratified by language, accent and code-mixing, and score each vendor’s WER and CER per slice, plus accuracy on the things that matter: amounts, policy numbers, names and plan names. Compare English-first, multilingual and Indic-tuned models such as IndicConformer, Sarvam, Bhashini, Google and Azure on that set, and weigh accuracy against cost, hosting and data residency. A clean wideband benchmark or a single blended number is not enough.
Callers switch between Hindi, English and Tamil. What changes in the speech pipeline?

Identify the language on every turn, or use a recogniser that handles code-mixing, instead of fixing it at the start of the call. Keep the transcript in a consistent script so downstream steps and scoring agree, boost domain terms with custom vocabulary, turn spoken amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar” into numbers with rules, read them back in the caller’s language, and hand low-confidence turns to a person.
mis: Reporting one blended WER
Report WER and CER per language and accent, with the worst slice named
Trusting raw transcripts for amounts
Normalise spoken amounts with rules and read them back before acting

telephony.t: Media streams send 20 ms audio frames. How many frames arrive in a 3-minute call?
iv: How do you connect a voice agent to real phone calls?

Use a telephony provider with numbers or a SIP trunk, stream call audio (8 kHz μ-law) to the agent over a WebSocket or bridge SIP into a media server, handle DTMF, hold and hang-up, transfer warm to the contact centre with a summary, and log to the CRM.
What is a warm transfer?
Handing a call to a human along with context, such as intent, account and verification status, so the caller does not repeat themselves.
mis: Processing media in a distant region
Keep media near callers
Cold transfers
Pass a summary to the human

gloss: computer use
A model controlling a computer through screenshots and mouse and keyboard actions.
grounding
Mapping an instruction to the right element or coordinates on screen.
accessibility tree
A structured view of a page’s elements with roles, names and states, used by assistive technology.
aria snapshot
Playwright’s compact text view of the accessibility tree for part of a page.
cascaded voice pipeline
Speech-to-text, then an LLM, then text-to-speech, each streaming.
speech-to-speech model
A model that takes audio in and produces audio out directly.
turn detection
Deciding when the caller has finished speaking; also called endpointing.
barge-in
The caller interrupting while the agent is speaking, and the agent stopping to listen.
WER
Word error rate: the share of words a speech recogniser gets wrong.
code-mixing
Switching between languages within a sentence, such as Hindi and English.
OCR
Optical character recognition: turning images of text into text.
allowlist
The only domains or actions an agent is permitted to use.
OSWorld
A benchmark of real desktop and web tasks in virtual machines with scripted success checks.
WebArena
A benchmark of 812 web tasks on self-hosted sites such as shops, forums and GitLab.
pass^k
The share of tasks an agent passes on all of k repeated runs; a measure of reliability.
language identification (LID)
Detecting which language is being spoken, ideally on every turn, so the right recogniser and reply language are used.
inverse text normalisation
Turning spoken forms into written ones, such as “saadhe teen hazaar” into ₹3,500 or “double nine” into 99.
custom vocabulary
Phrase hints or a trained lexicon that make a recogniser prefer domain words such as plan names and policy terms.
narrowband audio
Telephone audio sampled at 8 kHz, which carries sound only up to about 4 kHz and loses detail that wideband models rely on.
SIP trunk
A connection carrying phone calls over the internet between a telephony provider and your systems.
DTMF
Keypad tones pressed during a call, used for menus and entering numbers.
warm transfer
Handing a call to a person together with a summary of the conversation.

header.lede: Agents are learning to see screens, click through apps and hold spoken conversations. Build them to act reliably, answer within a caller’s patience in Hindi and regional languages, read documents and photos carefully, never act on instructions hidden in a page, and prove they work on your own tasks rather than on a public benchmark score.
